title: Spike a typed provider registry covering one provider's launch contract
description:
Objective: find out whether provider launch policy can be centralized before anyone commits to moving 11,000 lines of Bash and PowerShell. The roadmap calls a typed provider registry the enabling refactor, and also warns against a wholesale launcher rewrite before a vertical slice proves the contract.

Deliverable: a written decision plus a typed registry definition covering one provider only. Add a provider descriptor type naming argv and config construction, session mode, event capabilities, resume support, terminal handoff and failure classification, populate it for a single provider, and add contract tests asserting the descriptor reproduces the argv and config that scripts/moe-agent.sh and scripts/moe-agent.ps1 build for that provider today. Record the findings in docs/plans as a dated decision note: what the descriptor covers, which provider-specific exceptions resisted it, and whether a staged migration is worth doing.

Not in scope: changing any launcher behaviour, migrating a second provider, or moving the launch state machine into Node. The wrappers must be byte-for-byte unchanged in what they actually execute.

Verification: the new contract tests, plus bash scripts/tests/parity-check.sh and bash scripts/tests/postflight.sh proving the launchers still behave identically.
definitionOfDone: A typed provider descriptor covers argv and config construction, session mode, event capabilities, resume support, terminal handoff and failure classification
The descriptor is populated for exactly one provider and contract tests assert it reproduces that provider's current argv and config from both wrappers
A dated decision note lands in docs/plans stating what generalized cleanly, what did not, and a recommendation for or against a staged migration
No launcher behaviour changes: bash scripts/tests/parity-check.sh and bash scripts/tests/postflight.sh both pass unmodified
The contract tests run in an existing suite rather than introducing a new test runner
taskRails: Spike only: the wrappers' executed behaviour must not change in this task.
One provider. Migrating a second is a follow-up decided by this task's note.
No new test runner or build tool.

implementationPlan.description: SCOPE THE SPIKE AND PICK THE PROVIDER. Read-only, no edits. This is a decision task: the deliverable is knowledge plus a small typed artifact, and the launchers must end byte-identical. (a) Establish the central constraint before designing anything: neither wrapper has a dry-run or print-argv mode. Confirm it - the only argv introspection in scripts/moe-agent.sh is the codex probe around lines 5251-5264, which appends --help to the real argv to make the CLI short-circuit, and there is no flag that prints the argv without launching. Consequence: a contract test cannot execute a wrapper to capture argv, so it must assert against the scripts as text, the way scripts/tests/parity-check.sh already extracts and compares string vocabularies across both files. That limitation is itself a finding for the decision note. (b) Choose ONE provider and record why in the step note. The recommendation is codex, because it exercises all six descriptor facets with evidence that already exists in the repository: two session modes (the interactive terminal default and the exec headless path), real config construction in .codex/config.toml including mcp_servers entries, a startup timeout, a reasoning-effort key and a tools-approval pin, sandbox argv that differs per platform, and a genuine failure classification in the argv probe that stops a seat with a named code instead of relaunch-looping. The claude provider is a worse first choice precisely because its two wrappers diverge most - one runs in the launcher directory with a temporary config, the other changes directory and merges a user-level file - and the spike should learn whether a descriptor handles the ordinary case before the hardest one. If exploration changes your mind, say so in the note and proceed. (c) Read that provider's construction sites in BOTH scripts end to end and list, literally, every argv fragment, environment key, config key and failure code it builds. (d) Confirm whether docs/plans exists and how existing notes there are named and dated. (e) Record the git status baseline for the two wrapper scripts so step 5 can prove they are untouched.

implementationPlan.description: DEFINE THE DESCRIPTOR AND POPULATE IT ONCE. Create packages/moe-daemon/src/providers/providerDescriptor.ts. It lands in the daemon package for one reason only - that is where TypeScript types and the existing vitest suite already live - and the file's header comment must say plainly that the location is PROVISIONAL, that nothing imports it, that the daemon does not and must not launch agents, and that where this belongs if the migration proceeds is one of the questions the decision note answers. Define a descriptor type with one member per facet the Definition of Done names: argv construction, config construction, session mode, event capabilities, resume support, terminal handoff and failure classification. Two design rules matter more than the field names. First, model the two wrappers explicitly rather than pretending they agree: any facet that differs between the bash and PowerShell launchers is represented as a per-wrapper value, not flattened into one - a descriptor that silently hides a divergence would be a false positive for the whole spike. Second, the descriptor is DATA describing what the wrappers do, not policy they consume: no function that builds a command line, no branching logic, nothing importable that could tempt a later change to start driving behaviour from it while the scripts still own it. Populate it for exactly the provider chosen in step 1, transcribing what the scripts actually build today - not what they ought to build. Where a facet genuinely has no answer for that provider, encode an explicit unsupported or unknown value with a comment naming the reason; leaving a field blank or inventing a plausible value would corrupt the finding. Error handling for this artifact is the type system plus the contract test: the descriptor must not be constructible with a facet omitted, so every member is required.

implementationPlan.description: PIN THE DESCRIPTOR TO THE SCRIPTS WITH A CONTRACT TEST. Create packages/moe-daemon/src/providers/providerDescriptor.contract.test.ts in the existing vitest suite - a task rail forbids a new test runner, and vitest is already the daemon's. The test reads scripts/moe-agent.sh and scripts/moe-agent.ps1 off disk, resolving the repository root from import.meta.url the way src/tools/registry.test.ts resolves its own directory, and fails loudly with the resolved path if either file is missing rather than passing vacuously - a contract test that silently finds nothing is worse than none. Assertions: every argv fragment, environment key, config key and failure code the descriptor declares must actually appear in the wrapper it is attributed to; a facet the descriptor marks as shared must appear in BOTH scripts; and a facet marked as diverging must appear in one and not the other, which is the assertion that stops the descriptor from quietly papering over a difference. Add the negative direction as far as it is honest: for the one vocabulary that is already enumerable, assert the descriptor declares no failure code the scripts do not contain. Be explicit in a comment about what this test can and cannot prove - it proves the descriptor's strings are present in the launchers, not that the launchers assemble them in that order, because no dry-run mode exists to ask. State that limitation here and again in the decision note rather than letting a reader assume the stronger guarantee. Keep the matching literal and anchored; a loose substring match that accidentally succeeds on a comment line would make the whole spike untrustworthy. Run npx vitest run src/providers/providerDescriptor.contract.test.ts from packages/moe-daemon and require green with nonzero counts. Sanity-check the test's own power by temporarily corrupting one declared fragment in a scratch copy and confirming it fails - restore it immediately, and never mutate the shared checkout peers are working in.
implementationPlan.note:
Contract test strengthened, then PROVEN by deleting every emitter line in both wrappers.

Test changes:
- joinBashContinuations(): moe-agent.sh's bash view joins `\`-continuations (and collapses the surrounding whitespace), so a four-line launch invocation is one matchable string. PowerShell's launches are single lines, so its view is deliberately left untransformed rather than run through a normalizer that could only add false matches.
- New assertion "every emitted fact declares per-wrapper emitter evidence": every SHARED fact under config., argv.tokensByMode. or argv.perSeatOverrides must carry emitterEvidence for BOTH wrappers, each literal >=12 chars and present at the codex site. A new config fact cannot skip the stronger pin - the requirement itself is asserted (50 emitter literals checked; lower bound pinned at 30).
- New assertion "pins each session mode to its own whole launch invocation": exactly two modes, one launch literal per wrapper per mode, and no literal reused across modes (a shared launch literal would prove nothing about either mode).
- Fact-count lower bound for divergent raised 12 -> 14 after the project_doc reclassification.
- UNPINNED_NOTES const + a test that it is non-empty: states plainly that PowerShell's splatted $codexSeatArgs cannot be pinned per mode, and that facts outside the emitter-pinned prefixes (banners, sandbox vocabulary, resume, escalation text) are branch-presence only. implementationPlan.description: WRITE THE DECISION NOTE, WHICH IS THE ACTUAL DELIVERABLE. Create a dated note in docs/plans named for the provider-registry spike, following whatever naming and dating convention step 1 found there. It must answer four questions honestly, including when the answer is unflattering to the idea. What generalized cleanly: which facets transcribed into the descriptor with no loss for this provider. What resisted it: every place the two wrappers diverge, every value that is computed at runtime from the environment rather than fixed, every provider-specific exception that needed its own field or an unsupported marker, and the fact that no dry-run mode exists so a descriptor can only be pinned by text presence rather than by executing the launchers and comparing real argv. What it would cost: an honest estimate of extending this to the remaining providers given that the two scripts together run to roughly eleven thousand lines, and which of them look hardest and why - name the claude wrapper divergence and the grok constraints as the known hard cases. And a recommendation, for or against a staged migration, stated as a recommendation rather than a decision, with the smallest next step that would raise confidence - the obvious candidate being a print-argv mode in both wrappers so a future contract test could compare real command lines instead of text fragments, which is deliberately NOT done here because this task must leave the launchers untouched. Record the provider chosen and why, and note that the descriptor's location in the daemon package is provisional and load-bearing on nothing.

implementationPlan.description: PROVE THE LAUNCHERS DID NOT MOVE, THEN RUN THE GATES. The headline rail is that the wrappers' executed behaviour must not change, so prove it first and directly: `git diff --stat -- scripts/moe-agent.sh scripts/moe-agent.ps1` must be empty against the baseline recorded in step 1. A descriptor that required editing a launcher to make its test pass would have failed the spike, not the launcher. Then run the three gates from the repository root. The daemon suite: npm --prefix packages/moe-daemon test, Windows npm.cmd, filtering for the summary lines but capturing the exit code in a separate statement because a filtered pipeline swallows it; require exit 0 and confirm the new contract test was actually collected by the normal run rather than only by an explicit path. Then bash scripts/tests/parity-check.sh and bash scripts/tests/postflight.sh, both unmodified. Run the two harnesses sequentially on an otherwise quiet box and set MOE_POSTFLIGHT_TIMEOUT_SEC=180 - the default per-wrapper sixty seconds flakes while the fleet is running its own test suites, and the heartbeat-sidecar check is the first to go. If a harness fails, capture the shortest decisive line and diagnose rather than re-running blindly, and never pipe through grep with pipefail set, which turns a failure into a silent exit code. Record every command, exit code and count for the verification argument of complete_task.

implementationPlan.description: ADVERSARIAL REVIEW AND HANDOFF. Review the spike as a sceptic whose job is to stop a bad refactor from being greenlit on weak evidence. Does the contract test actually fail when the descriptor is wrong - you checked that in a scratch copy, so say so with the specific fragment you corrupted. Could any assertion pass against a comment line or an unrelated occurrence rather than the real construction site? Does the descriptor flatten any genuine divergence between the two wrappers into a single value? Does any field contain what the scripts ought to build rather than what they do? Is the note honest about the limitation that text presence is weaker than argv equality, and does it say so in the recommendation rather than burying it? Does anything import the descriptor, and does the daemon remain state-only with no launch behaviour added - an epic rail. Confirm the two wrapper scripts are still byte-identical to the baseline and that exactly one provider was covered, since migrating a second is explicitly a follow-up this note is supposed to recommend or reject. Then complete through moe.complete_task with the recorded gate evidence and every created path in modifiedFiles. Lead the completion summary with the recommendation itself, for or against a staged migration, because that sentence is what this task exists to produce - the type and the test are supporting evidence for it, not the point.
implementationPlan.note:
Adversarial review, answering the step's own questions.

Q: Does the test fail when the descriptor is wrong? Yes, with named fragments. `approvals_reviewer=user` -> `owner` fails shared-presence; a divergent bash-only literal swapped for `MOE_DAEMON_HOST` (present in both) fails the asymmetry assertion; flattening daemonHostUpsert to shared fails the fact-count and emitter assertions; an invented failure code fails the negative-direction assertion; deleting emitterEvidence from config.tables[0] fails the new requirement. All in a throwaway worktree, all restored, all re-verified green.

Q: Could an assertion pass against a comment or an unrelated occurrence? Full-line comments are stripped; ps1 is asserted to have no block comments. Matching is site-scoped, and the emitter tier goes further. Proven, not argued: deleting the emitting line of all 46 emission sites turns the suite red. The CONTROL mutation (weaken to whole-file, delete ps1's codex [mcp_servers.moe]) stays GREEN, which is what shows site-scoping still does work. Trailing inline comments still survive stripping - stated in the header.

Q: Does the descriptor flatten a divergence? 14 divergent facts, each asserted present at its own site and absent from the whole other file. project_doc_fallback_filenames was the one flattened fact QA found; it is now divergent, re-simulated independently here over three inputs.

Q: Does any field say what the scripts OUGHT to do? The EXIT-trap cleanup claim was exactly that and is corrected, with a comment in the descriptor telling the next transcriber to follow the code, not the comment. The daemon-host entry no longer asserts a PowerShell behaviour that does not exist.

Q: Is the note honest about text presence vs argv equality, in the recommendation? Yes - recommendation reason 1 now says what the strengthened pin still cannot catch (reordered flags, tokens that never reach the child, values wrong after expansion), rather than leaving it in a footnote.

Q: Imports / daemon stays state-only? grep for CODEX_DESCRIPTOR|providerDescriptor outside src/providers across packages and moe-vscode/src: 0 hits. grep for spawn|execFile|child_process|simple-git|git inside src/providers: 0 hits. Descriptor is pure data; the three `if (` hits in it are quoted PowerShell source inside string literals, not TS logic.

Q: One provider? src/providers/ holds exactly codexDescriptor.ts, providerDescriptor.ts and the test; the suite asserts the populated set equals ['codexDescriptor.ts'].

Q: Launchers byte-identical? sh f64bdb88272f01b5904ea895211e0730c5e23716, ps1 f456b7d14e05c42307e6dd515863a8cdfaf367e2, and git diff --stat over both launchers AND both harnesses is empty.

Residual weaknesses I chose to state rather than fix, all disclosed in the test header, the ArgvFacet comment and the note: (1) text presence is not argv equality, and no dry-run mode exists to close it - that is the note's central recommendation; (2) PowerShell's splatted $codexSeatArgs cannot be pinned per mode; (3) twelve branch-present shared facts are not emitter-pinned because none of them is written to a config file or argv; (4) divergent facts are emitter-proven by measurement, not by the type system; (5) trailing inline comments survive stripping; (6) the four GLOBAL_FACT_PATHS facts are whole-file matched because their evidence genuinely lives outside any provider branch.

Checklist items that do not apply and why: no concurrency (module-level synchronous reads of two files, no shared mutable state); no untrusted input (the inputs are two repo files and a const); no side effects or writes at all; missing-file handling throws loudly with the resolved path rather than passing vacuously, and a deleted-between-check-and-read file also throws. One theoretical residue: joinBashContinuations would splice across a full-line comment sitting between a `\` and its continuation body - that shape does not occur in moe-agent.sh today and the suite would go red if it appeared.

Last edit this step: tightened the UNPINNED_NOTES doc comment (it said "asserted nowhere" while a test does keep it non-trivial), and corrected the artifact table's line count for the test file to 411. Re-ran: contract test 23 passed exit 0, npx tsc --noEmit exit 0.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered: Executing the wrappers in a dry-run mode and diffing real argv - rejected because no such mode exists, and adding one would edit both launchers, which the headline task rail forbids; the note recommends it instead as the smallest next step that would raise confidence. Writing the contract test in bash beside parity-check.sh - rejected because the descriptor is required to be typed, so the test that pins it should read the same TypeScript value the descriptor exports rather than a transcription of it. Creating a new package for the registry - rejected: heavier than a spike warrants, and a task rail forbids a new build tool; the daemon package is chosen only because vitest and the type system already live there, and the header comment and the note both record that the location is provisional. Flattening wrapper differences into one value per facet - rejected as the single most damaging thing this spike could do, since the whole question is whether launch policy generalizes, and hiding a divergence would answer it falsely. Covering a second provider to strengthen the sample - rejected by a task rail; whether to do that is precisely what the note recommends or rejects.
planningNotes.codebaseInsights: The decisive fact, measured on 2026-09-11: neither wrapper has a dry-run or print-argv mode. The only argv introspection anywhere is the codex probe in the bash wrapper around lines 5251-5264, which appends --help to the real argv so the CLI short-circuits before any model call - it exists to detect a rejected flag, not to expose the command line. So a contract test cannot execute a launcher and compare real argv; it can only assert that the strings the descriptor declares are present in the scripts. scripts/tests/parity-check.sh is the precedent for exactly that shape: it extracts code families, banners, settings keys and environment names from both files and fails on any asymmetry. codex is the recommended subject because the repository already documents its full contract across all six facets - two session modes, config.toml construction with mcp_servers entries and a startup timeout and a reasoning-effort key and a tools-approval pin, per-platform sandbox argv, and a real failure classification in the probe that stops a seat with a named code rather than relaunch-looping. The claude provider is the known hard case and a poor first subject: its two wrappers diverge most, one running in the launcher directory with a temporary config and the other changing directory and merging a user-level file.
planningNotes.risks: The main risk is a spike that flatters the idea. A contract test asserting loose substrings would pass against comment lines and make a shaky descriptor look proven, so matches must be literal and anchored, and the worker must verify the test actually fails when a declared fragment is corrupted - in a scratch copy, never in the shared checkout peers are working in. The second risk is scope drift: the launchers must end byte-identical, so step 5 checks that directly with a diff against the step 1 baseline rather than assuming it. Nothing may import the descriptor; the daemon stays state-only. Test-environment quirks on this box: run parity-check and postflight sequentially on a quiet machine with MOE_POSTFLIGHT_TIMEOUT_SEC=180, because the default sixty seconds flakes while the fleet runs its own suites and the heartbeat-sidecar check fails first; and never pipe a harness through grep with pipefail set, which converts a real failure into a silent exit code. Finally, the note must stay a recommendation, not a decision - this task has no dependents and exists to inform a choice someone else makes.

completionSummary:
RECOMMENDATION (the deliverable): AGAINST starting a staged migration of launch policy into a typed provider registry now. FOR one narrow prerequisite first - a print-argv mode in both wrappers - which is deliberately NOT done here because it would edit a launcher. Full argument in docs/plans/2026-09-11-provider-registry-spike.md; the type and the test are supporting evidence, not the point.

Why: codex launch VOCABULARY generalises almost perfectly (30 of 44 transcribed facts shared - sandbox modes, failure codes, config keys, the exec argv skeleton), but launch POLICY does not. 14 of 44 facts diverge, ~32%, on the provider chosen because it was expected to be the easy one. Five are behavioural - the proxy-command block shape, the PowerShell prompt quote guard, TOML value encoding, startup-timeout validation, and the project_doc_fallback_filenames merge fix-up - and a sixth is a feature asymmetry (daemon-host discovery exists only in bash). Centralising means picking a winner on each, which is a behaviour change wearing a refactor's clothes. And none of it can be verified today: with no dry-run mode a contract test can only assert text, never argv equality.

REOPEN PASS - all nine QA issues fixed:
- Test blind spots closed and PROVEN. SharedFact gained per-wrapper `emitterEvidence`; the test now REQUIRES it (41 literals) for every fact written into .codex/config.toml or onto argv, and pins each session mode to its WHOLE launch invocation as one literal (bash continuations joined). 46 delete-the-emitter mutations, 22 in moe-agent.sh and 24 in moe-agent.ps1, ALL RED - including the five QA showed staying green (sh:876, sh:881, sh:891, sh:907 and sh:5303, the interactive -c MOE_WORKER_ID). A deliberate CONTROL mutation (weaken back to whole-file matching, delete ps1's codex [mcp_servers.moe]) stays GREEN, proving site-scoping is still load-bearing.
- Note accuracy fixed. Divergence #1 no longer claims ps1 has daemon-host discovery - it is reclassified as a feature asy

issues.description: Site-scoped presence is still satisfied by lines that emit nothing. In a worktree at 63ce155, each mutation that deletes an EMITTING line stays 20/20 GREEN: M8 sh:876 "[mcp_servers.moe]", / M2 sh:891 "[mcp_servers.moe.env]", / M10 sh:907 "[mcp_servers.serena]", / M9 the sh:881 startup_timeout_sec append. Cause: strips() repeats the headers (sh:935/937 header.startswith), and sh:871 names the python var startup_timeout_sec. ps1 is immune only because its matchers are escaped regexes.

To pass: deleting the emitting line of any config fact must turn the suite red, in EACH wrapper. Use evidence only the emitter contains (per-wrapper evidence for shared facts is fine) or a narrower emission sub-site. A fact that honestly cannot be pinned by text must be named in the test header and the note, with the green bash rows added to the red-proof table (note lines 87-92). Also fix note line 31 ('pins each one at the codex construction site of both files').

tokensByMode is not pinned per mode. M6 deletes the interactive launch's -c "mcp_servers.moe.env.MOE_WORKER_ID=$WORKER_ID" (sh:5303) and stays GREEN, because the exec launch (sh:5288) and the probe (sh:5259) carry the same literal. Add mode-unique evidence per wrapper (e.g. the interactive line's -C "$PROJECT" "$SHORT_PROMPT"). Otherwise, state in the ArgvFacet comment, the test header and the note that a token dropped from one mode goes undetected.

Divergence #1 is false: moe-agent.ps1 has NO daemon-host discovery. It only reads $env:MOE_DAEMON_HOST (ps1:752, 1013) and never assigns it. The only discovery is the bash cross-boundary WSL probe (sh:1336-1361, export at sh:1356), which the sh:1454-1507 upsert persists. A PowerShell run that discovers the host at probe time cannot happen, and both wrappers write a pre-set host (sh:897-898, ps1:752/769). In CLAUDE.md, 'both TOML writers' means the codex and grok writers inside bash.

Fix: call divergence #1 a feature asymmetry, in the divergenceReason here and in the note. Cross-boundary discovery is bash-only, so there is no winner to pick and no latent ps1 bug. Then update everything that counts it: 'five behavioural divergences' (note lines 45-51), recommendation reason 2 (line 122), follow-up 1 (line 134) and the summary counts.

The bash cleanup value says 'again by the EXIT trap'. That is false. Every create_secure_temp call runs in $(...) (e.g. sh:5147), so SECURE_TEMP_DIR is set only in a subshell. cleanup_temp's rm -rf (sh:142-144) is a no-op, and each call leaks a mktemp dir. Repro: X=""; f(){ [ -z "$X" ] && X=$(mktemp -d); echo "$X"; }; a="$(f)"; b="$(f)"; echo "$a $b [$X]" prints 2 dirs and an empty X. The sh:5310-5312 comment is wrong; record what the code does. The leak itself is out of scope.

project_doc_fallback_filenames is marked SHARED, but its merge fix-up diverges. Bash replaces only the exact string project_doc_fallback_filenames = ["CLAUDE.md"] (sh:955-959). ps1 regex-rewrites any list containing "CLAUDE.md" (ps1:824-826). Simulated on existing configs ["CLAUDE.md", "AGENTS.md"] and no-space project_doc_fallback_filenames=["CLAUDE.md"]: ps1 adds .codex/agent-instructions.md and bash does not. That is the note's own keys-match-values-drift lesson.

Fix: reclassify project_doc_fallback_filenames as divergent, with literals that pass the asymmetry check. Update the counts everywhere: 31/13 becomes 30/14, and 13 of 44 (~30%) becomes 14 of 44 (~32%). That covers note §1 (this line), §2, the behavioural list, and the test's lower bounds if needed.

Minor: 'every TOML string value is escaped through json.dumps' is not quite true. developer_instructions interpolates role raw (sh:860). That is harmless because sh:318 validates role, but reword it to something like 'every operator-controlled value'.
